en: Preface to the *Abridged Commentary on Amitābha*:

To conceive the thought of Buddhahood in a single moment, and to perceive all Buddhas by relying upon one Buddha—what teaching could surpass this as a gateway to the principle of mindfulness of the Buddha?
To invoke a single name is to embody ten thousand virtues; to attain one single-holding is to encompass a hundred.
To practice is not merely to uphold the name; who else can transcend this?
To behold the six directions from a single location and to comprehend all teachings through a single teaching—were it not for the scriptural tradition of Amitābha, who could be so wondrous as this?
To enter the stage of non-retrogression upon hearing a single word and to realize Bodhi by believing in a single matter—were it not for Śākyamuni... [this would not be possible].

Regarding the exposition of the fruit: who is capable of reaching such a state? Therefore, from the site of enlightenment at Vajrāsana until the twin śāla trees, our World-Honored One spoke only the teaching of the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*).
Beginning with the *Avataṃsaka* and concluding with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he extensively expounded the Dharma-gate of the Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti*) at Rājagṛha for the sake of Vaidehī.
"This mind is the Buddha; this mind creates the Buddha. When the bodies of all Buddhas enter the arising mind, [it is thus].

The Buddha-body is the very manifestation of the mind of sentient beings. When sentient beings contemplate the Buddha-body with their minds, the arising of that mind is itself the radiance of the bodies of all Buddhas.
Thus spoke the Jeta Grove to Śāriputra: To hold the Name, one takes single-mindedness and single-purpose as the goal;

to attain rebirth, one takes the three types of wisdom and the three kinds of merit as the core principle; to establish the circumstantial retribution, one takes practice, vows, and virtuous nature as the essence; and for the primary retribution, one takes...
The fruit of enlightenment is supreme. Since one takes self-nature as Amitābha, one likewise takes the mind-only as the Pure Land.
When the mind is defiled and evil, it is the suffering Sahā world; when the mind is pure and good, it is the blissful Land of Peaceful Nourishment. When the mind is perverse and deluded—

This is precisely what is called the "sentient being," for their mind is the perfect awakening. This is precisely what is termed the "Buddhas," for the teaching-net of the jeweled bells covers the trees of the seven factors of enlightenment;
the diamond-cord of the precepts intersperses the steps of the eightfold noble path. The lotus of the knowledge of all modes blooms in the waters of virtue;

the pavilion of the true mark soars high above the emptiness of nature. The music of the Dharma resounds in the heaven of the ultimate truth; the rain of awakening flowers falls upon the ground of the reality-limit.

The six stages of existence are eloquently expounded as the five faculties; the three types of mind-born beings serve ten thousand Buddhas. The joy of dhyāna satiates the life of wisdom, and the robe of patience is draped upon the Dharma-body.
As the masters of the transformative path, their lights shine in mutual radiance; for ten kalpas they do not depart from the present thought-moment.
The holy beings in their final birth before Buddhahood never regress; the ocean of fruition returns to the source of the cause. In seven days, they return to the one mind;
through the three ranks, they ascend through the nine grades. This mind and this principle are fundamentally identical; the original Buddha and the other Buddhas praise each other in turn.
One should believe that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable. One must know that the teacher of the Dharma is rare and exceedingly difficult to encounter;

it is for this reason that Yunqi composed these commentaries and sub-commentaries. He embodies the Buddha and embodies the sutra, accords with the capacities of beings and accords with principle, and every word accords with the fundamental nature.
All phenomena return to one’s own mind. The sovereign mind is the teacher; the mental factors are the disciples. Ultimate truth is the Śrāvaka; conventional truth is the Bodhisattva.
Initial awakening merging with original awakening is what our Buddha praises as Amitābha. Original awakening merging with initial awakening is what all Buddhas praise as Śākyamuni.
When ultimate awakening is perfected, it is called "The Buddha Speaks. Having finished speaking the sutra, [the light] pervaded everywhere.
He did not remain, but instead paid his respects and departed. In this manner he annotated the sutras, elucidating them wherever he went.

These expositions of the meaning all possess textual authority and serve as a mirror for reflection. Since the time of the Seventh Patriarch of Mount Lu, they have propagated the single gate of the Pure Land.
There has never been a work that surpasses this one. If one practices according to these teachings, there is no conduct that is not encompassed;

if one realizes the truth by relying on these principles, there is no fruition that is not fully attained. (Continuation of the Dharma) Having received [this grace] most deeply, I shall repay it by transmitting the lamp.

I have excerpted passages according to the text and titled them with brief annotations, so that they may be widely propagated through successive generations and extensively expounded throughout the world. Beginning with the elementary studies, one shall investigate the Great Learning, and subsequently...

Furthermore, one realizes the stage of the advanced practitioner. Regarding the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance: it is the remembrance of the Buddha and the remembrance of the mind. Regarding the single practice of pure karma: it is the purity of nature and the purity of the land.
Having already made vows, and now making vows, one aspires to attain the non-retrogressive mind and enter the stage of non-retrogression.
Whether in this life or in future lives, upon birth one shall behold Amitāyus and achieve infinite radiance. Four-colored flowers will be fragrant [around them].
The Lotus Pond: May the fragrance of the fruit of these seven trees pervade the net of flames, universally transforming all sentient beings so that they may together journey to the Land of Bliss.
With this heart of truthful speech, I set it forth at the beginning.
Written by Xufa, a member of the sixty practitioners from Ciyun Monastery in Hangzhou, Zhejiang,
on the anniversary of the Buddha’s birth during the Qinghe month of the Gengchen year of the Kangxi reign, at the Venerable Chamber of Chongshou Monastery in Longgang.
*A Brief Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha*.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xufa of Guanding at Ciyun Temple on the River Zhe, Qing Dynasty;
annotated by the Śramaṇa Yan Guang of Yingbi at Baoguo Temple on Fengling.
This sutra has been divided into ten sections for annotation.
△ First, regarding the causes for the arising of the teaching, there are both general and specific aspects.

The general aspect is that the Tathāgata appears in the world solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition (*ekamahā-kāraṇa*), desiring only to cause sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*).

This present sutra directly points out that sentient beings may enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through the mind of *nien-fo* (recollection of the Buddha). The specific aspects are tenfold; the first is the exhortation.
1. To inspire ordinary beings by arousing a sense of joy in the pure and aversion toward the defiled; 2. To admonish and encourage those of the Two Vehicles so that they may cultivate the Pure Land;
3. To lead those entering the Mahāyāna forward so that they may attain the Buddha-way; 4. To universally encompass the three grades of practitioners so that all may attain deliverance; 5.

To urge and exhort those in the eight difficult conditions so that they may transcend them and enter the state of sainthood; 6. To uniquely take pity on those in the Dharma-ending age and act as a bridge and raft for them; 7. To stand out specifically above all other gates.

First, because it is a skillful means. Second, because it directly points to sentient beings to simply recite the Buddha’s name. Third, because it further clarifies that holding the name is the path within paths.
Fourth, because it skillfully demonstrates the fulfillment of vows and practices to attain rebirth.

△ Second, the classification of the two collections and the vehicles (*piṭaka-yāna-vibhāga*). There are two [types of] collections: first, the three collections (*tri-piṭaka*), namely Sūtra, Vinaya, and Śāstra;

these are subsumed within the Sūtra-piṭaka. Second, the two collections, namely Śrāvaka and Bodhisattva; these are subsumed within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. The vehicles are also twofold: first, the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*).
Small, medium, and great. These are subsumed within the Mahāyāna. Second, there are the four vehicles: Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, Bodhisattva, and Buddha.

These are subsumed within the Buddhayāna. When divided, there are twelve types: prose (sūtra), verse (geya), prophecy (vyākaraṇa), isolated utterance (udāna), spontaneous discourse (nidāna), and causal narrative (itivṛttaka).
The *avadāna*, *itivṛttaka*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, and *upadeśa* have not yet appeared. The prose (*gadya*), the *udāna*, and the two divisions [of verse] are subsumed [within these].

△ Regarding the three periods of the assembly, first distinguish between the preceding and subsequent times, opening them into three: first, the time when the sun first shines; second, the time when the sun rises and shines further;
this is further divided into three, namely the initial turning, the middle turning, and the final turning. Third, the time when the sun sets and shines again.
This present sutra belongs to the second, the middle turning, within the period of the rising and shining. Next, the general explanation.
At that time, ten [points] are opened: first, regarding only the duration of a single thought-moment; second, encompassing the entire period of one cycle of transformation;
third, pervading all three temporal limits; fourth, including kalpas of the same category; fifth, including kalpas of different categories; sixth, subsuming kalpas within a thought-moment;
seventh, the mutual inclusion of kalpas and thought-moments; eighth, the kalpas of realms of different categories; ninth, the mutual inclusion of these [realms].
Tenth, regarding the period when the root encompasses the branches: this present sutra, from the *Avataṃsaka* up to the *Samantabhadra’s Vow King*, leads one back to the Land of Bliss;
from the *Lotus Sutra* up to the "Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja," one encounters Amitābha; and during the remaining nine periods, [the same applies].
The Dharma-door of Mindfulness of the Buddha was taught with fervent intensity and without interruption. Later, there were five assemblies: first, the Avataṃsaka and Brahmajāla assemblies;
second, the Saṃyukta Āgama assembly; third, the Saṃdhinirmocana Vaipulya assembly; fourth, the Prajñāpāramitā of Sublime Wisdom assembly;
and fifth, the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka and Mahāparinirvāṇa assembly. This [teaching] was spoken during the time of the Vaipulya assembly.

△ Regarding the fourth section, the "Delimitation of the Meanings of the Four Teachings," the teaching is divided into two parts. First is the teaching on the transformation of the Dharma, which is further divided into five: 1. the Small Teaching; 2. the Initial Teaching;
3. the Final Teaching; 4. the Sudden Teaching; and 5. the Perfect Teaching. It is subsumed under the Perfect Teaching here, as it pertains to the One Buddha Vehicle.
Because it is praised by all Buddhas; because it is a sutra of inconceivable merit; because by recollecting the name of a single Buddha, one universally perceives all Buddhas;
furthermore, it belongs to both the sudden and the final [teachings]. It is "sudden" because this mind is the Buddha, and because one swiftly realizes Buddhahood in a single thought-moment.

It is "final" because this mind creates the Buddha, and because one ultimately attains Buddhahood. Next, regarding the teachings of the transformative ritual, there are ten [aspects], the first being the beginning and the end.

1. The gate of differentiation; 2. The gate of the fundamental giving rise to the derivative; 3. The gate of subsuming the derivative back into the fundamental; 4. The gate of the non-obstruction between the fundamental and the derivative;
5. The gate of indeterminacy according to capacity; 6. The gate of the simultaneous manifestation of the exoteric and esoteric;

7. The gate of instantaneous, simultaneous exposition; 8. The gate of silent stillness beyond words; 9. The gate of universal penetration throughout the three periods of time; 10. The gate of infinite, layered profundity.
This is subsumed under the primary dharma within the first section on distinctions.

From beginning to end, it is solely for the sake of those with the capacity for the One Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*), as it expounds the perfect and sudden teaching (*samyak-akṣepa-śāsana*) of the Buddha-remembrance method (*buddhānusmṛti*). It also concurrently encompasses the latter two [sections], as it provides inexhaustible teachings throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions.
Its meaning is also twofold. First, regarding the four types of Buddha-remembrance: first, reciting the name; second, contemplating the image; third, contemplating the visualization.

Regarding the four aspects of the true mark (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*), Qingliang (Zongmi) expanded them into five: first, the gate of reciting the name and being born in the Pure Land through mindfulness of the Buddha; second, the gate of extinguishing transgressions through mindfulness of the Buddha by contemplating the image;
third, the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha as the subsumption of objects within the mind alone; fourth, the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha where mind and object are non-obstructive;

and fifth, the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha as the perfect interpenetration of dependent origination. The first two constitute the contemplation of the phenomenal realm (*dharma-dhātu*) of events, while the latter three constitute the true mark of the mind-only (*citta-mātra*).

The contemplation of the principle-dharma-realm (*li-fajie*) involves the contemplation of mental images; it is the contemplation of the non-obstruction between mind and phenomena, and the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena.

There are five gateways of dependent origination, which constitute the contemplation of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena. Now, in clarifying the practice of holding the name, five gateways are likewise opened:

1. The gateway of mindfulness through reciting the name while grasping it: this involves the notion that the Buddha’s name and form exist outside the mind; it belongs to the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) and is the contemplation of the phenomenon-dharma-realm (*shi-fajie*). 2. The gateway of subsuming the name back into... [text truncated]
The first is the Mind-Recollection Buddha-Gate. The name of the Buddha is manifested solely by the mind; this is the Initial Teaching (*śāstra*).

It is the Contemplation of the Principle-Dharma Realm (*dharmadhātu*) through the Three Minds, called the "Mutually Fusing" Mind-Recollection Buddha-Gate, wherein the mind is itself the Buddha; this is the Final Teaching (*śāstra*). The fourth is the Mind-Recollection Buddha-Gate of the Total Extinction of All Minds.
"Neither mind nor Buddha" refers to the Sudden Teaching (Ton-gyo), which is the contemplation of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (ri-sa mu-ae kwan).

"The single thought-moment of the fivefold, infinitely layered, inexhaustible gate of mindfulness of the Buddha," wherein the name of a single Buddha universally encompasses the Dharma-realm and its dependent origination is inexhaustible, refers to the Perfect Teaching (Won-gyo), which is the contemplation of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (si-si mu-ae kwan).
Thus, this single practice of mindfulness of the Buddha samādhi (nien-fo hang-sam-mae) includes all five teachings and penetrates the four dharmas.
The meaning and principles of the realms are profound and vast; this can well be understood.

△ Fifth, the preliminary selection of the grades of those to be benefited: Those who possess the three wisdoms of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, and are fully equipped with the three provisions of faith, aspiration, and practice, are all termed "suitable vessels.
Conversely, those who lack these are not of the proper capacity. Furthermore, among those who are vessels, there are three [grades].
The classes are divided into nine grades; each grade is further subdivided into immeasurable categories. Next, they are collectively gathered together.

Whether one harbors doubt or faith, whether one slanders or praises, provided one hears and knows the name of that Buddha, one will certainly be born in that land and shall all attain the Way of Buddhahood.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; those who possess Buddha-nature shall all become Buddhas. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* (Da-ben) says: "The earth..."
Even the ghosts of hell and the animals are born within my land; thus, whether they are characterized by love or hatred, compliance or opposition, all are the karmic conditions for the Buddha.

△ Sixth, the classification of the essence of the teaching according to its depth and shallowness, divided into four parts. First, the Gate of Following Phenomena (Suixiangmen), which further has two aspects:

first, that which refers to sounds, names, phrases, and syllables; second, that which refers to the principles and meanings they express. Since both text and meaning belong to the realm of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*), this is so called. Second, the Gate of Consciousness-Only (Weishimen). This text...

This meaning is that all are transformations of consciousness. Regarding the gate of the three natures: previously, the myriad objects transformed were subsumed back into the eight transforming consciousnesses;
now, the eight consciousnesses manifested are further returned to the single nature that manifests them. This is the gate of the four non-obstructions.

Mind, phenomena, principle, and events have been mutually penetrating from the very beginning. Phenomena and events follow after appearances; the mind is mere consciousness; and principle returns to the nature.
Because they are mutually fused and encompassing.
△ Seventh, the scope and limitations of the various tenets: there are six schools in total. First, the School of Phenomenal Adherence to Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-dharma-abhiniveśa-vāda*);

this is the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) school found in the *Āgama Sūtras* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. Second, the School of Yogic Practice of Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra-lakṣaṇa-yogācāra-vāda*); this is found in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

1. The School of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Mahāyāna. 2. The School of Emptiness and Signlessness (*śūnyatā-nimitta*) of the Threefold Truth. [Texts: *Suvikrāntavikrāmī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. This is the School of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the Mahāyāna. 3.

The School of Dependent Origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of the Matrix of the Store (*tathāgatagarbha*). [Texts: *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, *Ratnagotravibhāga-mahāyānottaratantra-śāstra*. This is the School of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) of the Mahāyāna.
4. The School of the Quiescence of True Nature (*bhūtadhātu-nirvāṇa*). [Texts: *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*. This is the School of Non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*) of the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, the School of the Perfect Interfusion of the Six Dharma Realms, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra* belong to the One Vehicle Dharma Realm School (*Ekayāna Dharmadhātu*).
Devadatta’s practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, through which he universally beholds all Buddhas of the Dharma Realm, belongs to the Avataṃsaka School.

Śrī-Ālokakara’s entry into the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) by means of the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha belongs to the School of Non-nature (*Niḥsvabhāva*). Upon hearing the account of Bhaiṣajyarāja in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, [he] went to peace...

The Land of Bliss belongs to the Dharma-nature school (*dharmatā-yāna*). One should contemplate it in accordance with the Dharma. To specifically clarify this sutra, it is further divided into general and specific aspects.

Generally, its essential purport consists of the purity of the environment and its inhabitants, rebirth through faith and aspiration, and the attainment of non-retrogressive *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Specifically, five pairs are established: first, teaching and meaning; taking the words of the teaching as the vehicle, one realizes the intent of the meaning.

1. Events and Principle: Taking the characteristics of phenomena as the primary focus is the "event," while revealing the rational nature is the "principle. 2. Object and Wisdom: Taking the objective realm as the object of perception is the "object," while giving rise to contemplative wisdom is the "wisdom.
3. Practice and Stage: Taking faith, aspiration, and practice as the core is the "practice," while the nine grades of practitioners constitute the "stage.
4. Cause and Effect: Bringing the causal merits to fulfillment is the "cause," while realizing the virtues of the fruition is the "effect."
△ Section on the Differentiation of the Eight Classes has two parts: 1. The Great Canon; 2. This Sūtra. The classes are threefold: 1.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations); 2. The *Dundubhisvara-rāja-sūtra*; 3. The *Amitābha-gāthā-sūtra* (Later Translation). 3.
Those that are neither sections nor classes, such as the *Avataṃsaka*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Śūraṅgama*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-saṃyojana*, and the *Mañjuśrī-bhāṣita*.
If one includes the mention of the Pure Land and so forth.
△ Ninth, the general explanation of the title, divided into two parts:
first, the name of the sutra—The Buddha-spoken Amitābha Sūtra.

This brief outline has four parts: first, the Buddha who speaks; second, the actual exposition of the teaching; third, the Buddha spoken of; and fourth, the conclusion regarding the title of the discourse.
This refers to the sutra in which Śākyamuni Buddha of this land expounds upon Amitābha Buddha of that land, his pure land and its adornments, and the practice of rebirth through faith and aspiration.
To explain in detail: the Sanskrit term *buddha* is translated here as "the Awakened One" (*jue-zhe*). He is one who has awakened himself and awakened others.
Because it encompasses the beginning, the source, and the ultimate, the *Avataṃsaka* elucidates ten Buddhas; the *Laṅkāvatāra* elucidates four Buddhas;
and the *Cittabhūmi-darśana* elucidates three Buddhas, who are none other than our own teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha.

"To preach" (*śāsana*) is a Sanskrit term for *pratibhāna*, which here means "eloquent exposition," as it refers to the proclamation and unfolding of the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*). It also means "to gladden," as it brings joy to one's fundamental aspiration. This teaching extends through five [vehicles].

There are five types of persons: first, Buddhas; second, Bodhisattvas; third, devas; fourth, rishis; and fifth, emanated persons. To say now that "the Buddha spoke" is to distinguish him from the other four.
*A* in Sanskrit means "non-" or "without"; *mita* in Sanskrit means "measure. This refers to the Buddha's merit.
Because they are inconceivable: the teachings and meanings within the causal stage; principle and phenomena; the realm of wisdom; severance and realization; practices and vows; the stages and ranks;
causal cultivation; karmic fruition; essence and function; the inverse and the compliant; the wisdom and vows upon fruition; names and characteristics; radiance; lifespan; retinue; lands;
supernormal powers; preaching the Dharma; responsive manifestations; and benefits—all are without measure or number. Thus it is said in the *Píngděngjué jīng* (Sūtra of Equal Enlightenment).
It is translated as "Immeasurable Purity. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Chengzan jingtu jing) states: "Named Immeasurable Life and Immeasurable Light.
This merely cites one or two examples from the perspective of his fruition stage. The *Sūtra of the Names of Ten Thousand Buddhas* lists ten names:
Buddha Amitābha, Buddha Amitadhvaja, Buddha Amitaghoṣa, Buddha Amitapraśasta, and Buddha Amitanādita.
Amitakūṭa Buddha; Amitābhyudgata Buddha; Amitābhasiṃha Buddha; Amitābhasthita-dhāraka Buddha;
Amitābhābhyudgata-śreṣṭha Buddha. These twelve names appear in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*. [Also: Amitābha Buddha;
Anantābha Buddha; Apratihatabha Buddha; Apratihatābha Buddha; Arciṣmanta-bha-rāja Buddha; Viśuddhābha Buddha.

The Buddha of Joyful Light, the Buddha of Wisdom Light, the Buddha of Uninterrupted Light, the Buddha of Inconceivable Light, the Buddha of Incomparable Light, and the Buddha who Surpasses the Sun and Moon—these ten names sever the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*), the ten unwholesome actions, and the ten sufferings.

The twelve names cure the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and inverted perceptions regarding the six sense organs and six sense objects throughout the twelve periods of the day. "Immeasurable Purity" refers to the Great Body (*dharmakāya*). Dharma.

The Dharma-body Buddha (svabhāvakāya) is without beginning and without end; it is immeasurable life (*amitāyus*). This is the greatness of its marks (*lakṣaṇamahātmya*). The Reward-body Buddha (sambhogakāya) has a beginning but no end;
it is immeasurable light (*amitābha*). This is the greatness of its function (*vṛttimahātmya*). The Transformation-body Buddha (nirmāṇakāya) has both a beginning and an end.

First is the Self-nature body (*svabhāvakāya*), which possesses the virtue of great severance (*prahāṇaguṇa*) and is manifested by the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividhaśūnyatā*); it is identical for all Buddhas. Second is the Enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*), which possesses great wisdom (*mahājñāna*).

Virtue is true, eternal, and untainted; it is the shared intent of all Buddhas. The third [body] is the Nirmāṇakāya (Transformation Body), which possesses great beneficent virtue and manifests through meditative concentration and supernormal powers;
it is the common activity of all Buddhas. In the Sanskrit language, this is called *yukti-sūtra*;

here it is translated as "Sūtra of Accordance" (*qi jing*). *Yukti* means "accordance": it accords with the principle of Amitābha Buddha on the left, accords with the faculties and practices of sentient beings on the right, and accords with Śākyamuni Buddha in the center.

The six [meanings] are: Buddha, Fruit, Embracing, Sūtra, Scripture, and Discourse. Regarding the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, there are two meanings: first, "pervading," which refers to pervading the principles explained;
second, "sustaining," which refers to sustaining those beings to be converted. Herein, four meanings are clarified: first, "Eternal," meaning it is unchanging through antiquity and the present;

second, "Dharma," meaning it is equally honored by both the distant and the near; third, "Path," meaning the path for the transition between sentient beings and Buddhas; fourth, "Canon," meaning the sacred...

The "Worthy Text" (Xian-dian) provides an exegesis through a comparative analysis of dyads and their synthesis. There are four such pairs: 1. **The Dyad of Teaching and Meaning:** "Sūtra" (*jing*) refers to the teaching that expresses;

this constitutes the first five characters. "Meaning" (*yi*) refers to that which is expressed; this constitutes the subsequent five characters. 2. **The Dyad of Object and Wisdom:** "Buddha-spoken" (*fo-shuo*) refers to wisdom;

"Amitābha" (*Mito*) refers to the object. 3. **The Dyad of Essence and Function:** "A" signifies "non-"; it denotes the essence of the nature of non-arising. "Mita" signifies "measure"; it denotes the immeasurable.
Characteristics and functions; the four persons and the Dharma; the Buddha and the person; the teaching and the Dharma.
These are distributed across four gates: the Sūtra is the teaching; Amitābha is the principle; the teaching is the practice; and the Buddha is the fruit.

Six types of compound analysis (*ṣaḍ-vigraha*): 1. *Tatpuruṣa* (Dependent Compound): “The Buddha’s teaching” (*buddha-śāsana*). 2. *Karmadhāraya* (Appositional Compound): “The Buddha’s teaching, namely Amitābha” (*buddha-ukta-amitābha*). 3. *Śeṣa* (Possessive Compound): “There is a sutra taught by the Buddha concerning Amitābha” (*buddha-ukta-amitābha-sūtram asti*).

4. *Bahuvrīhi* (Exocentric Compound): “The Amitābha Sutra” (*amitābha-sūtraṃ*). 5. *Dvandva* (Copulative Compound): “Not the [treatise] of Vasubandhu” (*na vasubandhu-śāstraṃ*). 6. *Avyayībhāva* (Adverbial Compound):

A peak pavilion is called a *gé* (tower). The four staircases represent the four foundations of mindfulness (*śmṛtyupasthāna*: body, sensation, mind, and phenomena). The four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*: giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation). The pavilions and towers represent the three samādhis (*śūnyatā*, signlessness, and wishlessness).

The three types of dhyāna (*lokiya-dhyāna*, lokottara-dhyāna, and the supreme dhyāna). Gold represents the precepts (*śīla*). Silver represents faith (*śraddhā*). Lapis lazuli represents learning (*śruta*).
...Lapis lazuli is shame (*hrī*). Coral is progress (*vīrya*). Red pearl is wisdom (*prajñā*). Agate is relinquishment (*tyāga*).

Regarding "as large as a wheel," the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the golden wheel is fifteen *li* in diameter.
