*Kumuda* is translated as "yellow lotus. *Padma* is translated as "red lotus. *Puṇḍarīka* is translated as...
The white lotus: its eighty thousand petals are finely delineated, hence it is called "subtle" (*wei*); flower and fruit appear simultaneously, hence it is called "wondrous" (*miao*);

its filaments and pedestal emit a fragrance that perfumes the mouth, hence it is called "fragrant" (*xiang*); its roots and stems pass through without being stained, hence it is called "pure" (*jie*).

The lotus symbolizes the Buddha’s knowledge and vision within the *bodhi*-mind; the "great" symbolizes the One Great Buddha Vehicle (*ekayāna*) among the three vehicles. "Color" refers to the objective realm (*viṣaya*).

"Light" is wisdom (*jñāna*). It refers to the four gates of teaching, practice, fruit, and principle, as well as the four virtues beginning with subtlety (*sūkṣma*), which constitute the opening, revealing, awakening, and entering.
△ Next, the summary.
Śāriputra, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is adorned with such meritorious qualities.

To transform others through the Way is called "merit" (gōng); to realize reality within oneself is called "virtue" (dé). To have perfected the causes is called "accomplished" (chéng); to have fulfilled the fruits is called "attained" (jiù).

To fill the interior is called "adornment" (zhuāng); to manifest outwardly is called "splendor" (yán). Thus, when referring to the ponds, stairways, flowers, and pavilions, they are collectively termed "Adorned" (Mí).

He is one who has perfected the myriad virtues through the power of his vows and practices during the causal stage, and who has fully accomplished the adornment of the ten thousand merits of meditative concentration and wisdom upon the fruition stage.

As Amitābha’s vow states: "When I become a Buddha, throughout my land, from the ground up to the void of space, there shall be palaces and towers, ponds, streams, and flowering trees, all formed from hundreds of thousands of various jewels and fragrances. Those born in my land..."
All were born by transformation from lotuses within ponds of the seven treasures. It is further said that Dharmākara undertook the pure practices of twenty-one billion Buddha-fields;
having thus accumulated merit and virtue over immeasurable billions of kalpas, he finally attained perfect fulfillment and entered the rank of Buddhahood.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The practices of Samantabhadra’s ground of wisdom are all perfected; all adornments..."

"Adornment issues forth from this. This is said in reference to cultivation (*bhāvanā*). If explained according to the nature (*prakṛti*), then the great practices and great vows are all the untainted (*anāsrava*) merits of the Buddha's own nature.
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Within the Tathāgatagarbha, there are fully present meritorious qualities of the nature [of reality] as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "According to the purity of one's mind, so is the purity of the Buddha-field. Furthermore, the entirety of cultivation resides within the nature.

It is just as with "Virtue-Adornment" (*guṇavyūha*): through cultivation arising from the entirety of nature, this adornment of merit is accomplished; since nature and cultivation are non-dual, such an adornment of merit is thus achieved.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "All nets of precious bells arise from the mind that realizes all phenomena are like illusions;
all precious pavilions arise from roots of goodness that are unattached and from roots of goodness that are unborn."
It is further said: "In the ocean of the Flower Treasury World, every mountain, river, and forest is each called the True Suchness Dharma-realm, endowed with boundless virtues.
A verse says: "The Flower Treasury World-ocean / Is equal to the Dharma-realm without distinction; / Its adornments are utterly pure.
The following examples should be understood by analogy to this. Section Two: Heavenly Music and Rain of Flowers. Part One: Individual Enumeration.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, in that Buddha-land, celestial music is constantly played and the ground is made of gold. Six times throughout the day and night, it rains *mandārava* flowers.
The sentient beings of that land always at dawn each take a robe-sack filled with various wonderful flowers to make offerings to hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas in other directions;
then, at the time of the morning meal, they return to their own land to eat.

Regarding the practice of *caṅkrama* (walking meditation), there are five aspects of its meaning: first, celestial music; second, golden ground; third, rain of flowers; fourth, the three turns of the Dharma wheel; and fifth, the constant [practice]. "Music" symbolizes the dharma of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
"Golden ground" symbolizes the mind-ground of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. "Rain of flowers" clarifies the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. [The fourth aspect is] the four... [of the Dharma wheel].
There are four kinds: first, *māndārava*, which means "pleasing" or "white flower";
second, *mahāmāndārava*, which means "great white flower"; third, *mañjūṣaka*, which means "soft" or "red flower";
fourth, *mahāmañjūṣaka*, which means "great red flower. Day symbolizes the transformation of afflictions into bodhi; night symbolizes...

It transforms birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) into nirvāṇa. The six periods of the day symbolize the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) illuminating and shattering the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), thereby eliminating the six afflictions (*ṣaḷkleśa*).
The six periods of the night symbolize the non-arising of the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*) and the six perceptions (*ṣaḍsaṃjñā*), severing the impurities of the six doubts.

"Rain" signifies moistening and nourishing. "Heaven" signifies the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). The four flowers symbolize the causes of the four stages: abiding, practice, orientation, and the grounds (*vihāra-caryā-mukha-bhūmi*). The four magnificent offerings [symbolize the fruits].

"Sentient beings" refers to those from the time after the Buddha’s descent [into the world] down to the sages and ordinary people. "Early morning" is one of the six periods of the day. "Jinju" (襟裾) refers to the lap (*kaṭicāpa*), which serves as a vessel for holding flowers.
There are three kinds of exquisite flowers: first, celestial flowers; second, terrestrial flowers, distinguished by their growth on plants or trees;

and third, aquatic flowers. "Early morning" symbolizes original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). The "robe-lap" symbolizes the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The assembly...
Flowers represent the three practices: namely, seeking Bodhi above, cultivating the Six Perfections in the middle, and transforming sentient beings below.
Offering to the Buddha signifies adorning the fruit with causes. The internal inclusion of "informing the Buddha" regarding other regions represents not only self-awakening but also awakening others.
Regarding the five types of food: the time for eating is morning, which represents the "name-awakening" within initial awakening; midday—

"Similar awakening" (*sadr̥śa-bodhi*) refers to the time when the sun has declined; "partial awakening" (*anurūpa-bodhi*) refers to the late afternoon; and "perfect awakening" (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) refers to the evening.

"One's own country" (*svadeśa*) refers to the realm of one's own true nature (*svabhāva*). "Returning" (*pratyāgama*) represents the three bodies of meaning and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*). Regarding the *Āgama-sūtras* and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, they clarify the five supramundane nutriments (*āhāra*):

first, the nutriment of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*); second, the nutriment of mindfulness (*smṛti*); third, the nutriment of the joy of dhyāna (*dhyāna-prīti*); fourth, the nutriment of the joy of the Dharma (*dharma-prīti*); and fifth, the nutriment of liberation (*vimukti*). As the treatise says:

One delights in the flavor of the Dharma and takes the samādhis of dhyāna as food. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "The nectar of the Dharma is the food; the flavor of liberation is the drink.

"Practice" (*xing*) signifies the three types of beneficial conduct (*trividha-karman*). Furthermore, "food" (*shi*) signifies meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is the realm of self-awakening. "Practice" (*xing*)—[refers to]... [the three types of beneficial conduct].
"Manifesting wisdom" refers to the contemplation that awakens others. △ Second, the summary:
"Śāriputra, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is thus adorned with the accomplishment of such meritorious virtues."
The Vow of Amitābha states: "Those among humans and devas who hear my name shall offer lamps and scatter flowers.

Bodhisattvas who offer incense, flowers, and other offerings to the Buddhas of the various directions shall have them reach [the Buddha] everywhere within the time it takes to eat a meal. When it is time for food and drink, [these offerings shall appear] within a precious bowl."

A hundred flavors appear before them; once they have eaten, [the food] departs of its own accord. It is further said that some become bhikṣus or universal monarchs who constantly go to the Buddha’s presence to make offerings.
From their hands, food, clothing, banners, canopies, music, and so forth constantly emerge.

Thus we know that the flowers, food, and clothing of Sukhāvatī arise spontaneously—all of which are brought about by the power of Amitābha’s vows and practices. △ Fourth, the transformed birds and winds.
Second, the trees. First, listing and clarifying the two [categories]. First, the transformation birds expounding the Dharma.
Third, the initial formal presentation: Furthermore, Śāriputra, in that land there are always various wondrous and multicolored birds:
white cranes, peacocks, parrots, śāris, kalaviṅkas, and jīvañjīvakas. These various birds, day and night, six times...

At that time, he uttered a harmonious and elegant sound. That sound expounded and elucidated the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and such dharmas as these.

"Four" is repeated as "again. "Next" refers to what follows. As for the various birds: the eighty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) *pāramitā* dharmas are represented by them. The white crane represents the *śīla-pāramitā* (perfection of ethical discipline);

it is pure white and unstained. The peacock represents the *dāna-pāramitā* (perfection of giving); its variegated plumage brings joy to people. The parrot represents the *kṣānti-pāramitā* (perfection of patience);

it is kept as a pet by others. The *śāli* bird is the same as the *sārasa* crane; it represents the *vīrya-pāramitā* (perfection of vigor), supporting the aged with its labor like a hoe or a sickle. The *kāka* [crow]..."

*Laṅkāpāda* (陵頻伽). This is translated as "Immortal Sound" (*xiānyīn*) or "Exquisite Sound" (*miàoyīn*). Regarding the *dhyānapāramitā*: before emerging from its shell, its voice surpasses that of all other birds.
In Sanskrit it is *jīvajīvaka*, which is translated as "Shared Life" (*gòngmìng*) or "Life-Life" (*mìngmìng*).

It further says, "Life-giving life. Having one body and two heads signifies the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); having attained the life-force of wisdom, there is no obstruction between the provisional and the ultimate.
The three periods of the day manifest the opening of the three causes of Buddha-nature and the purification of the three karmas. As for the three periods of the night:

To dwell in silence within the secret treasury of the three virtues is to extinguish the three obstructions. In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), this is called "Harmony" (he); in the Sudden Teaching (Dunjiao), it is called "Refinement" (ya).
To spread and proclaim is "Exposition" (yan); to open and clarify is "Fluency" (chang). That which can give rise to the holy path is "Root" (gen); that which grows and establishes it is "Power" (li).

These five are, in total, the one [set of] faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. The seven parts are the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyanga): discrimination, and so forth.

Vigor, joy, equanimity, relinquishment, concentration, and mindfulness. The Eight Noble [Factors] are the Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right vigor.

"Mindfulness" refers to concentration (*samādhi*). "Equal" (*sama*) points to the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that assist the path, as well as morality (*śīla*), concentration, wisdom (*prajñā*), the noble eightfold path, and even the truths, the bases of power, and the perfections (*pāramitā*). △ Next, the benefits are revealed.
When the sentient beings in that land hear this sound, they all bring to mind the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.

The sound [proclaims] the primary and auxiliary paths of practice. The Buddha possesses the three bodies and four wisdoms; the Dharma consists of teaching, practice, principle, and fruition; the Sangha comprises those on the stages of fruition and approach among the noble ones.

To "bring the Buddha to mind" is to contemplate his grace in severing delusions and realizing the truth, as well as his benefit in bestowing bodhi. To "bring the Dharma to mind" is to transcend birth...
The benefit of Nirvana is the grace that delivers one from death. The benefit of liberation is the grace that enables one to leave suffering and attain happiness.
△ Next, resolving potential objections:
"Śāriputra, do not think that these birds are truly born as a result of their karmic retribution for sins. Why is this? That Buddha..."
In that land, there are no three evil realms. Śāriputra, in that Buddha-land, even the names of the evil realms do not exist, let alone their actual presence.
All these various birds are transformations produced by Amitābha Buddha, intended to cause the sounds of the Dharma to circulate.
First, I shall resolve the doubts and difficulties. A doubt arises: "For what reason are there animals in the Pure Land? To this, the text replies: "Do not harbor such a thought.
Those born there as a result of karmic retribution for their sins—those who were deluded fall among animals; those who were stingy and greedy fall among hungry ghosts."
Those who kill out of anger fall into hell. Furthermore, the ten grave evils (*daśākuśala*) and the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) of the superior grade result in retribution in hell;
those of the middling grade result in retribution as hungry ghosts (*preta*); and those of the inferior grade result in retribution as animals (*tiryagyoni*).
As the verse of Dharmākara says: "Hell-beings, ghosts, and animals shall all be born within my land; all who come to be born there cultivate pure conduct. Thus it is.
The Buddha’s golden body possesses all the wondrous marks in their full perfection; thus one knows that women who are born in the Western Land possess the marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
Those born in the three miserable realms who attain Sukhāvatī obtain the retribution of Buddhahood. Second, the reason for this is set forth in two parts.
First, the miserable realms do not truly exist there; as the Vow of Dharmākara states: "In my Buddha-field, there shall be no ghosts or animals."
It extends even to the wriggling insects. It is further said that among the people within this land, no one hears an evil name, much less possesses its reality;
therefore, there are no three evil paths, nor even the names of unwholesome things. Regarding the phrase "these various [beings] below," they are manifested through the power of the two Buddhas.
There are two meanings to this: first, the Tathāgata’s supernatural power manifests birds to preach the Dharma; second, it is the mutual cultivation of causal natures upon the fruition.

Form and mind melt away. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "The King of Wish-Fulfilling Jewels emits subtle, golden light, which transforms into birds of a hundred precious colors, warbling in harmonious and elegant tones, praising the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. △ Second, the winds and trees expound the Dharma.
Śāriputra, in that Buddha-land, when a gentle breeze stirs the rows of jewel trees and the jeweled nets, they produce a subtle and wondrous sound,
like hundreds of thousands of kinds of music playing simultaneously. Those who hear this sound naturally give rise to thoughts of mindfulness of the Buddha,
mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Saṅgha.

First, the emergence of the Dharma-sound, which is twofold; this is the first [aspect] of the Dharma. "Subtle" (*miao*) means subtle, cool, clear, and pure; it is profound, harmonious, and pervasive. There are eight [aspects] to its opening:
first, gain; second, non-decline; third, non-reproach; fourth, good reputation; fifth, praise; sixth, absence of censure; seventh, freedom from suffering; eighth, happiness.
Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of the "Eight Winds" (*aṣṭau vāyavaḥ*) according to the Wei translation, they are described as gentle and subtle, and harmonious.

Harmonious; neither cold nor hot; temperate and cool; supple and soft; neither slow nor rapid. The *Contemplation Sūtra* states that the eight kinds of pure winds represent the inconceivable teachings, practices, principles, and fruits of the Dharma.
Wind symbolizes the characteristic of emptiness—the path of the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle according to the Nature School (*Xingzong*).
The trees are the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*); the nets are the seven great natures; and the sounds are the eight [liberations].

"Sound" refers to the four types of eloquence (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*). "For example" introduces the two metaphors. "A hundred thousand" refers to the musical scales of humans and devas, which represent the ten dharma-realms (*daśa-dharmadhātu*):

namely, teaching and meaning, principle and phenomenon, object and wisdom, practice and stage, cause and effect, person and dharma, the dependent and the primary, essence and function, and the inverse and the compliant.

"Responsive resonance" (ganying) constitutes the ten pairs of dharmas. "Acting together" possesses the ten mysterious gates (shixuanmen). Regarding "hearing [the teaching]" below: second, this reveals the benefit of hearing;
the Buddha is like a king of physicians, the Dharma is like excellent medicine, and the Sangha is like a nurse. Third, as for "awakening the mind":

when the *shijue* (initial awakening) mind opens, the nature of the phenomenal dharma-realm (*shi-fajie*) becomes manifest; this is the benefit of mindfulness of the Buddha. When the *benjue* (original awakening) mind opens, the nature of the noumenal dharma-realm (*li-fajie*)...

To attain manifestation is the benefit of mindfulness of the Dharma. The beginning and the source are unified; the perfectly wondrous awakened mind manifests as the nature of the dharma-realm where phenomena and principle are without obstruction—this is the benefit of mindfulness of the Sangha.
It is further said: "Those who see this tree attain the three dharmas of patience (kṣānti), forever sever ignorance, and realize the principle of the dharma-body;
this is called the patience of non-arising. This is the benefit of attaining Buddhahood. Hearing the holy teachings of the Buddha illuminates...

To clarify one's original nature is called the "Patience of Resonance" (*ghoṣānugā-kṣānti*); herein one obtains the benefit of the Dharma. To subdue afflictions and accord with True Suchness (*tathatā*) is called the "Patience of Accordance" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*);
herein one obtains the benefit of the Saṃgha. Since the benefits of hearing and seeing are thus, the benefits of awakening and knowing may be inferred accordingly.
△ Next, the conclusion.
Śāriputra, that buddha-field is adorned with such accomplished merits and graces.
Thus, it is like the sounds of birds and the voices of trees. As stated in the vows of Dharmākara: "When I become a buddha, the flowers and trees in my land shall [emit sounds of the Dharma]."
Immeasurable varieties of miscellaneous jewels and hundreds of thousands of kinds of incense were combined together to form it;

its fragrance universally permeated the worlds of the ten directions, and all sentient beings who smelled it cultivated the practices of the Buddha. It is further said that the Bodhi tree at the Buddha’s place of enlightenment was adorned with various jewels.
A jeweled net covers it above. As a gentle breeze stirs it, it produces the sounds of immeasurable sublime Dharma that pervade all Buddha-fields.
Sentient beings who hear them attain the profound *dharmakṣānti*, abide in non-retrogression, and proceed until they achieve unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Part Two: The Primary Retribution (the physical manifestation) has two sections. First, the Teacher has two parts. First, the inquiry into his name.
"Śāriputra, what do you think? For what reason is that Buddha named Amitābha? This inquiry has two intended meanings:

first, although the name was previously mentioned in brief, its specific significance and characteristics were not detailed; second, since the explanation of the meaning is now extensive, the same applies to its formal characteristics.
Therefore, he asks, "How is this so? △ Next, the manifestation of his virtues has two parts: first, how the single name contains two meanings. First:
"Immeasurable Light.
Śāriputra, the light of that Buddha is immeasurable; it illuminates the lands of the ten directions without obstruction.
For this reason, he is named Amitābha.
"Abundant light" refers to the fulfillment of wisdom. This means the light of knowledge, the light of the body, the constant light, and the radiating light.
Its causes are twofold: first, it is accomplished through ten thousand virtues; second, it is brought about by original vows. Furthermore, "radiance" is the single path of true, authentic wisdom.
"Shining upon the world" refers to the wisdom of immeasurable skillful means (*upāya*). "Unobstructed" refers to the wisdom of the non-obstruction between the provisional and the real.
As for the mention of the "ten directions," this refers to the three vehicles and the seven destinies. According to the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, these are:

knowing all Buddhas, the Buddha-dharma, sentient beings, worldly phenomena, the three periods of time, the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the immeasurable, the boundless, and that which fills all worlds, abiding and sustaining them.
It is the wisdom that shines universally. △ Second, Infinite Life:
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the lifespan of that Buddha, as well as that of his people, shall endure for immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Therefore, he is named Amitābha (Immeasurable Light).
"Many years" refers to the fulfillment of his lifespan. The initial repetition of the word "also" (*yòu*) seems to be misplaced in the text;

it should read: "The lifespan of that Buddha and his people. Furthermore, regarding the term "people" (*mín*): because he is a Dharma-King, [he has subjects]. *Asaṃkhyeya* is translated as "innumerable."
The Buddha’s lifespan is threefold. For the *dharmakāya*, the true nature of reality (*tathatā*) constitutes its life; therefore, it is immeasurable.
For the *saṃbhogakāya*, wisdom and virtuous marks constitute its life; therefore, it is boundless. For the *nirmāṇakāya*, compassionate application constitutes its life; therefore, it is innumerable.

Furthermore, for the *nirmāṇakāya* that corresponds to the sages of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the lifespan is immeasurable; for the great transformation [bodies] corresponding to those prior to the ten stages—the three levels of worthiness (*tri-śuklavidhāna*)—it is likewise immeasurable.
As for the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), their lifespan is boundless. For those who manifest as lesser humans and devas, their lifespan is incalculable.

The *Cittabhūmi-darśana-sūtra* states: "Since the conditions of sentient beings are inexhaustible, the manifestations of response and transformation are uninterrupted; thus, they abide eternally in succession—this is the lifespan of the three Buddhas."
All are of infinite measure. There are also two causes for this: first, the fulfillment of the power of the original vow; second, the accomplishment through the power of merit.
Regarding the lifespan of the people, there are likewise two causes: first, the power of the Buddha’s original vow; second, the power of their own merit.
First, by holding the name of the Buddha, one extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas; therefore, it is "innumerable" (*asaṃkhyeya*).
By contemplating the image, the extinction of sin is limitless; therefore, it is "boundless" (*ananta*). By contemplating the marks and signs and their radiance, the extinction of sin is peerless;

therefore, it is "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*). Furthermore, because one seeks upward with a straightforward mind, it is immeasurable; because one practices with a deep mind, it is boundless; and because one transforms others below with a compassionate mind, [it is...]
Incalculable. Furthermore, by cultivating the three minds and three blessings in accordance with their true nature, one naturally attains a lifespan of boundless measure.
△ Second, the ten kalpas since the realization of the Way:
"Śāriputra, from the time Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood until now, ten kalpas have passed."

A doubt arises: "Since his lifespan is immeasurable, how many kalpas have passed from the time he attained Buddhahood until now? Therefore, this commentary explains: "More than ten kalpas have passed since the beginning;
from now on, he will remain in the world for further immeasurable and incalculable kalpas. In the Sanskrit language, this is called *kalpa*.
This is called "time-period" (*kalpa*). It is the great kalpa among great kalpas.

According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (The Scripture of the Names of Ten Thousand Buddhas), one kalpa of the Sahā world is equivalent to a single day and night of the Sukhāvatī world; thus, ten kalpas there surpass the countless kalpas of this world.
As for why it is said to be "ten," it signifies the uprooting of the delusions, karma, and suffering of the ten dharma-realms. △ Second.
The two types of transformed companions. First, the three vehicles in the present. First, the explanation:
Furthermore, Śāriputra, that Buddha has immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are arhats;
they cannot be known by means of calculation.

Furthermore, there are two tiers. "Śrāvakas" refers to those who hear the sound of the Four Noble Truths and attain the realization of the fruits; this includes both disciples (*śrāvaka*) who have mastered the path of the *pratyekabuddha* as well as those at the initial stage of training (*śaikṣa*).
"Arhats" specifically designates those at the fourth fruit who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). These constitute the assembly of the Two Vehicles.
"Bodhisattvas" refers to the assembly of the Three Worthies and Ten Grounds within the provisional and ultimate teachings of the Mahāyāna;

they are all boundless in measure and beyond calculation. This is because the Buddha, throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, cultivated the Truths, the Conditions, and the Perfections, extensively transforming sentient beings without end.
△ Next, the conclusion.
Śāriputra, that buddha-land is thus adorned with such accomplished merits.

Regarding the statement in the treatise that those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) do not take birth there: first, this refers to the stage of the causal ground; the *lakṣaṇa* school maintains that those of the two vehicles do not believe in the physical form of Buddhas in other directions.
Second, it refers to those who proceed directly [to enlightenment]. Third, it refers to those of definitive practice. As the sūtra says: "The śrāvakas are immeasurable."
First, regarding the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*): the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states that those of middle-high birth hear the Four Noble Truths and attain Arhatship;

those of middle-middle birth attain the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) in seven days and complete the four fruits in half an eon; and those of middle-low birth become Arhats in one small eon (*antarakalpa*).

Second, regarding the turning of the mind (*citta-parāvṛtti*). Third, regarding provisional transformation (*upāya-nirmāṇa*). As a verse cited from the East Sea (Korea) says: "The seven kinds of pure lotuses..."

It is thus that the multitude are born through transformation from the flowers of perfect enlightenment. As for the phrase "adorned with merit," this refers first to the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*).

The *Mahāvaipulya* [Sutra] states: "After Dharmākara had made his vows, for *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas he guarded his body, speech, and mind, practicing the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), realizing emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and through these practices he taught and transformed others, leading immeasurable sentient beings to resolve upon Bodhi."

Next, regarding the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*): the *Amitābha-sūtra* states that water pours between the lotuses and flows up and down the trees, proclaiming suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self, and the various *pāramitās*.
Furthermore, there are those who praise the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of the Buddhas.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Subtle ripples circulate in a swirling current, and waves raise sublime sounds. Some hear the sounds of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha;

some hear the sound of tranquility, the sound of emptiness and non-self, the sound of great compassion, the sound of the pāramitās, and the sounds of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
It further states: 'Once everyone has finished bathing, there are those on the ground who contemplate the Way, and those who practice walking meditation.'"
Those who preached the sutras in the void, those who practiced seated meditation, and those who had not yet attained the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path], thereby attained the four fruits;
those who had not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression as bodhisattvas, thereby attained the stage of non-retrogression.
Consequently, the lifespan of the people and the immeasurable [beings] of the Three Vehicles were all accomplished through the merit of Amitābha. △ Second, the sages and worthies who attain rebirth.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, those beings who are born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are all *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive).
Among them, there are many who are in their final birth before attaining Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), so numerous that they cannot be known by calculation;
they can only be described as immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*).

First is non-retrogression. The third section states: furthermore, sentient beings who vow to be born [in this land] from the ten directions are *avaivartika*. This is translated as the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*).
The *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra* explains that there are three types of non-retrogression: first, the bodhicitta of the Mahāyāna path does not retrogress of its own accord;

second, those who have already attained the stages of meritorious practice do not retrogress; and third, even those who have not yet attained the fruits of the realization of the noble ones (*ārya*) [do not retrogress].
"Non-retrogression" is explained here by encompassing both cause and fruit. In the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*, Xianshou explains it in three ways:

first, "non-retrogression" refers to being in a state where there are no conditions for falling back; second, "non-retrogression" refers to entering the stage of the right-determined group (*samyaktva-niyāma*) at the first abode;

third, "non-retrogression" refers to realizing the full dharmakāya at the first ground (*bhūmi*). This latter explanation applies across all five stages. However, the present sutra does not refer to any of these.

The second [interpretation] concerns the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*) as defined in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. From the first through the sixth stage, there is "non-retrogression in position" (*avivartana-sthāna*).

At the seventh stage, there is "non-retrogression in practice" (*avivartana-caryā*). From the eighth through the tenth stage, there is "non-retrogression in mindfulness" (*avivartana-smṛti*). Why is this so?

Because the former bodhisattvas already encompass all the stages prior to the [ten] stages, whereas the latter—the single stage of the "near-enlightenment" (*ekakalpa-avaśeṣa*)—is applied exclusively to the single stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyag-avabodha*). Thus, it is non-retrogression.

There are five causal conditions: first, being sustained by the power of compassionate vows; second, the constant illumination of the Buddha’s light; third, the preaching of the Dharma by the forest trees; fourth, having Bodhisattvas as companions;
and fifth, a lifespan lasting for eternal kalpas. The *Śāstra* states: "The assembly of humans, devas, and the immovable ones is born from the ocean of pure wisdom.

"Immovable" refers to the non-retrogressive stages (*avaivartika-bhūmi*). "Ocean of wisdom" refers to the ocean of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Next is the stage of the Regent (*ekajātipratibaddha*). First.
Regarding those who are "to be born" (upapadya): these are Bodhisattvas on the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi-bodhisattva*).

Because they are still separated from the ground of Buddhahood by one more birth, they sever this final portion of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and shatter this last grade of ignorance (*avidyā*). Like the moon at night, their light is utterly pure and full;

they then fill the rank of the Buddha, attaining the fruit of Perfect Wondrous Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-miśra-jñāna-phala*). As the Vow of Dharmākara states: "When I become a Buddha, the Bodhisattvas within my land..."
Their supernatural powers, wisdom, eloquence, and physical marks were all identical to those of the Buddha. Later, the numerical details are revealed:

the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* clarifies that within this world-system, seven hundred and twenty billion bodhisattvas, as well as bodhisattvas from fourteen buddha-fields in other directions and immeasurable other buddha-lands, have attained rebirth there.
It is through the three minds and four vows of the Buddha in his past lives that he was able to bring this about. △
Second, the section showing the seven periods for encouraging practice, which has four parts. First, the making of vows:
"Śāriputra, those sentient beings who hear this should make a vow, vowing to be born in that land. Why is this?
So that they may gather together in one place with such superior and virtuous people."
First, he exhorts them to generate the vow. Sentient beings are the "vessels" for the Pure Land;

within their *śruta-mayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from hearing) they contain the "requisite of faith," within their *cintā-mayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from reflection) they contain the "requisite of the vow," and within their *bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from cultivation)—which constitutes their lower wholesome virtues—they contain the "requisite of practice.

Apart from these three wisdoms and three requisites, one is not a vessel for the Pure Land. Regarding the phrase "those people below": this refers to the worthy and holy ones of the three vehicles mentioned above.
It is said: There are four benefits: first, one constantly hears the Dharma; second, one’s practice does not regress; third, there are no demonic obstacles;

and fourth, it is easy to enter the Way. In other lands, the opposite is true; therefore, one should aspire to and delight in this land. II. Initiating Practice (in two parts). First, the preliminary practices (*upāya-caryā*).
Śāriputra, one cannot be born in that land through few roots of goodness, merit, or causal conditions.

"Goodness" refers to the ten wholesome paths of action, the five faculties, and the first five perfections—these are practices for the benefit of others. "Virtue" refers to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)—this is the aspiration for one's own benefit.
Taking the internal, self-generated [realization] as the cause, one fully realizes that this very mind is the Buddha and gives rise to the bodhicitta.
The direct cause (*hetu*) is the manifestation of the nature. External assistance that brings it forth serves as the condition (*pratyaya*).

To realize that this very mind attains Buddhahood and to uphold the name of the Buddha is the manifestation of the conditional cause (*pratyayahetu*). "Not permissible" means admonition; "even a small amount" refers to accumulation.
Together these clarify the causes by which one attains the fruit. Next is the actual practice.
Śāriputra, if there are good men or good women who, upon hearing the teaching of Amitābha Buddha, hold fast to his name—
whether for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days—
with single-mindedness and without distraction.

The text has four meanings. First, it identifies the person and their faculties. Regarding the phrase "men and women are called 'good'": the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies that there are two types of Buddha-nature:

first, the Buddha-nature of principle (*li-fóxìng*); second, the Buddha-nature of practice (*xíng-fóxìng*). Thus, the goodness of the Buddha-nature refers to that which is inherently possessed; the goodness of cultivation refers to practice, which encompasses both the present and the past.
Next, it presents the Dharma-gate. To "earnestly hold [it] to one's heart" is called "clinging"; this refers to the bodily karma. From moment to moment, do not...

"Shi" (loss) is called "chi" (retention). In terms of verbal karma, there is further hearing; hearing-wisdom (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), grasping—contemplative wisdom (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), and retention—cultivational wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
There are four dharmas: first, clear recitation (*vācaka*); second, silent recitation (*manasā*);

third, half-clear and half-silent, reciting while slightly moving the lips and tongue, which in the tradition of mantra-reciters is called *vajra-dhāraṇī*; fourth, neither clear nor silent, abiding within the Buddha’s mind, luminously clear.

It is not obscure. The first three constitute the practice of maintaining the facts (*shih-ch'i*), which means that mindfulness is uninterrupted. The last one constitutes the practice of maintaining the principle (*li-ch'i*), which means contemplating the oneness of all things.
Among the various gates of *nianfo* (recitation of the Buddha's name), this specifically points to the single practice of the Samādhi of Holding the Name (*ch'i-ming i-hsing san-mei*).

Regarding the fixed duration of the period: the *Mo-ho pan-jo po-lo-mi ching* (Large Version) and the *Sheng-wang ching* specify ten days; the *Ta-chi ching* specifies seven weeks; and the *Pan-zhou san-meiching* specifies ninety days for those of dull faculties.

Too much. According to the *Sutra of the Fundamental Principle*, one day; according to the *Contemplation Sutra*, ten recitations; and according to the *Lotus Sutra*, a single invocation—these are for those of sharp faculties.
Too little. Now, seven days is the middle way. This signifies severing the afflictions of the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) by means of the seven consciousnesses.

(On Faith, the Ālaya, Karma, Transformation, Manifestation, Wisdom, Continuity, and the Manovijñāna): To remedy the seven branches of evil, one gathers the seven emotions; to transcend the suffering of the seven realms, one extinguishes the seven calamities.
This is like the first fruit of the path (*srotāpanna*) severing seven births; Kṣitigarbha’s determination of the seven weeks; the sovereign aligning with the seven administrative measures;
the *I Ching* noting that every seven days there is a recurrence; and even the seven-day gestation in the womb or the snake that slithers seven paces—it is all naturally so.

Furthermore, there are four aspects of accomplishing practice: single-mindedness. To encompass causal practice without distraction is to ensure that pure mindfulness continues uninterrupted through to the realization of the fruit;

this is single-mindedness in terms of phenomena (*dharma*). For mind and object to be non-dual is single-mindedness in terms of principle (*li*). To focus intently without delusion is non-distraction regarding phenomena.
To be in accord with reality as it is is non-distraction regarding principle. Alternatively, single-mindedness may refer to the principle of *nianfo* (recollection of the Buddha). This is the mind...

Because this is the Buddha, one accomplishes the samādhi of the single-practice true thusness (*tathatā*); this is concentration (*samādhi*). It is undisturbed; it is the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha through phenomena (*nimitta-buddhānusmṛti*).

Because this mind creates the Buddha, one accomplishes the dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha by holding the name; this is wisdom (*prajñā*). When these are combined, concentration and wisdom are equal.

This is the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle. If we follow the three-membered syllogism (*trirūpa-linga*) of the *lakṣaṇa-yāna* (Dharmalakṣaṇa school), it would be stated as follows: "The recitation of the Buddha's name" is the subject (*dharmin*).

"One-pointed mind without distraction" is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: "Because of single-mindedly maintaining [the practice] for seven days. The concordant example (*sapakṣa*) is: "Like the *mínglíng* caterpillar which, through a spell, becomes a wasp in seven days. △ Third, the realization of the fruit (*phala-pratilambha*).
When that person approaches the end of life, Amitābha Buddha, together with a multitude of holy beings, will appear before them.
At the time of death, this person’s mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.

Previously, the Buddha came to my place. That person was one who, in their daily life, was known as a name-holder. Regarding those for whom the Buddha appears at the time of death, Śrī-Ānanda (Shi-zhi) said:
"If you remember the Buddha and recite the Buddha's name, you will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future. "In the present" refers to within dreams or meditative concentration;
"in the future" refers to the stage of the empty mind-palace. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "All the sense faculties are completely dispersed and destroyed; only..."
This King of Vows leads the way before them; there is cause and there is effect. Thus, the Three Sages [appear] because of: first, the compassionate vows of the Three Sages;

second, what is elicited by the practitioner’s three minds, three practices, and three merits (as described in the *Contemplation Sūtra*). Next, regarding "I go to the Buddha’s place with an undisturbed mind":
since the cause consists of upholding the Name with a single mind without distraction, the fruit is the attainment of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection).
Regarding the practice of samādhi, Guishan said: "If one's thoughts are delusory and scattered during life, how can one attain a concentrated mind at the moment of death?
These three powers correspond as follows: one's own power of mindfulness is the inherent power of Buddha-nature; the assembly of holy ones is the power of the Buddhas' gathering-in.
Inherent nature is like a boat, mindfulness is like the sail and oars, and the Buddhas are like favorable currents and winds. Thus, one departs from birth and death.
"O Sea, reaching the shore is certain. Thus, for those who attain rebirth: if a person possesses virtuous aspirations, the Buddha will surely grant them;

if one recollects the Buddha by contemplating external objects, one will be born in a Pure Land of Transformation; if one recollects the Buddha by withdrawing objects into the mind, one will be born in a Land of Inferior Retribution;

if one recollects the Buddha through the mutual fusion of mind and object, one will be born in a Land of Superior Retribution; and when both mind and object are transcended, [one attains ultimate liberation].

By recollecting the Buddha, one is immediately born into the Buddha-land of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). By recollecting the Buddha with perfect penetration and inexhaustibility, one is immediately born into the Buddha-land of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "If one takes the Buddha as one's object and recollects him single-mindedly without ceasing, this person shall behold the Buddha."
Their number is equal to that of the mind; thus, the three grades and nine ranks respond with unfailing accuracy. △ Fourth, the conclusion on the benefits:
"Śāriputra, because I see these benefits, I speak these words. If there are sentient beings who hear this teaching, they should..."
One should make a vow to be born in that land.
"Benefit" refers to the advantage of being received by the Buddha at the end of life and thus attaining birth there. "Speech" refers to the words of single-mindedly holding the Name for seven days.
"Seeing" means beholding with one's own eyes; "speaking" means proclaiming with one's own mouth. "Hearing and Vowing" refers to hearing [the teaching] above and relying upon it.

The discourse on the adornment of true merit inspires the arising of aspiration and joy. This teaching on being received by the Buddha at the time of death through hearing and upholding his name encourages the cultivation of vows.
Hearing encompasses retention, reflection, and cultivation; aspiration includes faith and practice. Only when these six gates are complete is pure karma truly accomplished;
therefore, he exhorts them again to generate the resolve, clearly elucidating the benefits of the Dharma. There are ten aspects each for cause and effect. Regarding the ten benefits of the cause:
This means: a single name possesses myriad virtues; it is easy to practice at all six periods of the day; one may achieve success within seven days; in a single lifetime, one’s affairs are settled;
all transgressions are extinguished; all demons are kept at a distance; roots of goodness increase; one cuts across birth and death;

and the Buddha-nature is revealed. May the light of your vows receive me! As for the ten benefits of the fruit: the three sages come to welcome one; one departs for rebirth in the nine grades of lotus wombs.
Rebirth through transformation; attaining forever non-retrogression; a land pure and adorned; companions of sages and worthies; preaching the Dharma among trees and forests; an immeasurable lifespan;
personally receiving the Buddha’s prediction; and using supernatural powers to deliver sentient beings. △ Third, citing six Buddhas to accord with the principle, divided into two parts:
first, explaining the common praise of the Buddhas; second, the initial praise by the original Buddha.
Śāriputra, as I now praise the inconceivable benefits of the meritorious virtues of Amitābha Buddha—"I" distinguishes me from other sages and worthies;
"now" distinguishes this from the past and the future; "praise" distinguishes this from admonition or exhortation. It is not [a command].
"Contemplation" (*cintā*) excludes [merit] that has limited measure. "Virtue" (*guṇa*) excludes merit consisting of mere phenomenal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*).

"Benefit" (*artha*) excludes worldly advantage. To extol is called "praise" (*praśaṃsā*); to evoke renown is called "admiration" (*anuśaṃsā*). To awaken others is called "function" (*kārya*); to awaken oneself is called "virtue" (*guṇa*). There are twelve such virtues and benefits, namely:

basis (*āśraya*), correctness (*samyaktva*), name (*nāman*), body (*kāya*), light (*prabhā*), lifespan (*āyus*), lord (*adhipati*), retinue (*parivāra*), vow (*praṇidhāna*), practice (*caryā*), cause (*hetu*), and fruit (*phala*). As explained in the aforementioned sūtra.
△ Next, the praise by other Buddhas consists of six sections. First, three concerning the East. Initially, their names are listed to manifest their vastness:
In the East, there is also the Buddha Akṣobhya, the Buddha Sumerudhvaja, the Buddha Mahāsumeru, and the Buddha Sumeruprabha.
The Buddha of Wondrous Sound (Ghoṣadatta), and others such as these—Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—to the east.
"East" signifies movement; it is the head of all sprouting and movement, for from it all things grow and flourish. It corresponds to spring, the year, and the celestial stems *jia* and *yi*.

Wood, the corner, benevolence, and the origin—these are the initial manifestations of the *zhèn* (thunder/primordial movement). It is not only the Central [Direction] that is praised as the Śākyamuni;

there is also Akṣobhya, which is translated here as "Immovable. Because the Dharma-body is immovable, and because it darkly pervades the realm of myriad transformations, he is the Buddha of the Tathatā-body (*yǒurúshēn*).
Sumeru is translated here as "Wondrously High" (*miàogāo*). It is called "wondrous" because it is composed of the four precious substances.
Transcending the ten mountains is called "High" (Gao). The four virtues of *nirvāṇa* transcend the ten realms; therefore, it is named "Characteristic" (Xiàng).

This is the Buddha of the Body of Merit (*guṇakāya-buddha*). His marks and signs, as well as his radiance, are unsurpassed and supreme; he is thus titled "Great" (Dà). This is the Buddha of the Response and Transformation Bodies (*nirmāṇakāya-sambhogakāya-buddha*).

Because the eight consciousnesses are transformed, the four wisdoms are realized as the fruit; this is established as the name "Radiance" (Guāng). This is the Buddha of the Body of Wisdom (*jñānakāya-buddha*).

He preaches the Dharma with a single sound, yet beings understand it according to their own kind; this is called "wondrous voice. The preceding four [points] concern the body, while this concerns the vocal karma (*vākkarman*).

Thus concludes the pointing of the fingers. The phrase "and so forth" serves as an analogy for the remaining cases. Because he realizes the *saṃsāra*-like (infinite) inherent virtues of his nature, he consequently manifests Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
△ Next, he manifests signs to represent the Truth.
In each of their respective lands, they extend the mark of the broad and long tongue, completely covering the trichiliocosm.
"Broad" means it encompasses the ten directions horizontally; "long" means it penetrates the three periods of time vertically. Regarding its pervading the trichiliocosm:

according to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, even the tongue-faculty of ordinary sentient beings possesses one thousand two hundred merits; according to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, this is the case for Bodhisattvas of the Ten Practices.
They have accomplished the ten inexhaustible treasuries. When they preach the Dharma, they emit wondrous sounds from their broad and long tongues that fill all worlds throughout the ten directions;
how much more so for Buddhas at the stage of fruition! When they realize the Small Vehicle, [the tongue] covers the face and reaches the hairline;
when they realize the Great Vehicle, it covers the great trichiliocosm. It is as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where the broad and long tongue extends upward to the Brahma-heaven.
For a full hundred thousand years, he withdrew his tongue-organ, thereby manifesting the ten kinds of tongues that transcend the world.
Surpassing the nature, characteristics, causes, and effects of the three vehicles and the seven realms of existence, he proclaimed the supreme dharmas of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
△ Subsequently, he spoke words to exhort faith.
I speak these truthful words: you sentient beings should believe in this sutra on the inconceivable merit praised by all Buddhas, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
"Sincerity" (*cheng*) means not deceiving and not being otherwise. "Reality" (*shi*) means truthfulness and speaking according to reality.

"Sentient beings" refers to the assembly listening to the sutra from the nine realms in the various lands of the eastern direction. "Listen attentively" and "do not doubt" is called faith. "Praise" refers to Śākyamuni Buddha’s internal commendation and external proclamation.
"Virtues" refers to the meritorious achievements and deeds of Amitābha. "Protection and mindfulness" refers to the physical protection and mental recollection of all Buddhas.

"All" has three meanings: first, it specifically refers to the eastern direction; second, it generally encompasses the six directions; third, it extensively includes the ten directions throughout the three periods of time.
As the *Wenming* (Inquiry into Enlightenment) Verse states: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions share one and the same Dharma-body;
they are one in mind and one in wisdom, and likewise in their powers and fearlessnesses. Since this mind and this principle are identical, each Buddha [is thus the same].
This is a praise. As for the "Sūtra" (Jing): it serves as the path for the realm of sentient beings and constitutes the fundamental principle for Śākyamuni Buddha’s governance and management.
It is the eternal law of the Amitābha Sūtra and the way of the governance and organization of all Buddhas.

Vimalakīrti calls it the "Small Inconceivable," for the liberation of Vimalakīrti is intended solely for Bodhisattvas. The Avataṃsaka calls it the "Great Inconceivable," for the liberation of Vairocana...
It is liberated because it is the Buddha of Wondrous Enlightenment. The present sutra is likewise so, for it shares the same fruit as the Buddha.
Because sentient beings who mindfully recollect the Buddha perceive the Buddha-mind, they become Buddhas even while remaining ordinary beings; thus, faith encompasses the ocean of fruition.
How could such a Perfect and Sudden Great Teaching not be inconceivable? △ Second, the Southern Region has three parts. First, listing the names to manifest their vastness.
Śāriputra, in the world-systems of the southern direction, there are Buddhas such as Candrasūryapradīpa,
Yaśaḥprabha, Mahājvālāṃsa, Merupradīpa, and Anantavīrya— Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
South is brightness. South is the place where brilliance shines. The Sage faces toward the light to govern the world.
Summer, *ying*, *bing* and *ding*, fire, *zhi*, ritual, *heng*, and the sequence of abiding in *li*: these are the sun, moon, and lamps. The sun illuminates the day.

To shatter the darkness of views and afflictions is the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*). To illuminate the night like the moon, clearing away the dust and sand of delusions, is the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*).
To illuminate that which neither the sun nor the moon reaches, pervading both day and night and destroying all ignorance (*avidyā*), is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
That which is called "the light of renown" refers to the radiance of great wisdom that shines universally throughout the dharma-realm; therefore, it is given this name.
"Far-reaching hearing" refers to the Buddha’s wisdom of self-awakening. "This Buddha's awakening of others" refers to his wisdom of awakening others.

"Great Flame Shoulder" means that expedient wisdom illuminates phenomena while ultimate wisdom illuminates principle; it signifies bearing the entirety of the Buddha-dharma upon two shoulders from which flames issue forth.
"Sumeru Lamp" means that when expanded, it is the wisdom of the four dharma-realms, with lamps and lamps being inexhaustible; when contracted, it is the single reality free from obstruction.
The wisdom of the Dharma-realm is like the light of a single lamp, illuminating heaven and reflecting upon earth.

"Immeasurable diligence" refers to the three minds, the four vows, the six perfections, and the myriad practices—all of which are constantly pursued with diligence, without slackening or ceasing. The passage beginning with "Thus" lists names above;
this reveals their vastness. △ Second, manifesting signs to represent the True.
Each, within their own land, extended their broad and long tongues, completely covering the trichiliocosm.
△ Third, speaking words to exhort belief, he uttered these truthful words: "You sentient beings, you should believe in this praise of inconceivable merit. First.
From the *Sarvabuddhaparigraha-sūtra*, the Buddha addressed the sentient beings:
"There are two types of discourse: first, sequential guidance; second, simultaneous guidance.

This also refers to the fourfold assembly in their own lands in the southern direction and all those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha. Other cases follow this precedent; the subsequent sections should be understood accordingly. △
Third, the three [buddhas] of the western direction. First, listing their names to manifest their vastness:
Śāriputra, in the world-system of the western direction, there are the Buddha Amitāyus, the Buddha Amitābhavyūha, and the Buddha Amitadhvaja.

The Buddha of Great Radiance, the Buddha of Great Clarity, the Buddha of Precious Marks, the Buddha of Pure Light—such Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have all passed away to the West.
"West" is the precursor of change; therein all things undergo transformation and fall away. It is autumn, white, and associated with the *geng* and *xin* stems.
"Jin" (Metal), "Shang" (Trade), "Yi" (Righteousness), "Li" (Profit), and "Dui" (Joy) gradually diverge in meaning. Regarding the names of Buddhas who share the same root as Amitāyus:
Śākyamuni follows the ancient Śākya; Guanyin follows the ancient Avalokiteśvara.
There were twenty thousand Buddhas named Dīpaṃkara, five hundred named Samantaprabha, and two trillion named Meghasvararāja. These details are found in the *Wanshan* (Ten Thousand Mountains).

"Seeing all meanings" means that regarding the meaning of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) within all phenomena, there is nothing not known or seen to the ultimate degree; this is the realization of excellence.

Regarding the *Sūtra on Being Protected and Mindfully Remembered by All Buddhas*:
the reason for the mutual praise from the six directions is stated in the Vows of the Dharma-Treasury:

"When I become a Buddha, my fame shall reach the countless worlds of the ten directions, and each Buddha shall, amidst their own assemblies, proclaim my merits as well as those of my land. △ Second, the explanation.
The Sūtra reveals two benefits. First, it interrogates the name:
"Śāriputra, what do you think? For what reason is it called 'the Sūtra protected and remembered by all Buddhas'?"

Regarding the reason why the "inconceivable" is not asked about: it has already been explained and resolved within the "Praise by the Original Buddha," as it specifically points to the merits of Amitābha’s environment and its inhabitants (*śarīra-dharma*).
Regarding the reason why only "the Buddha’s protective mindfulness" is asked about: it was not mentioned previously;

here, it universally clarifies the merits of all Buddhas as well as the Dharma-benefits for sentient beings. △ Second, the explanation of the benefits, which is twofold. First, the benefits of the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Śāriputra, if there are good sons or good daughters who hear this sutra and accept and uphold it,
as well as those who hear the names of the Buddhas, all these good sons and good daughters shall be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas,
and they shall all attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
First, the name of the sutra that can be heard is set forth: "Good sons and daughters. Comparing the preceding and following sections, the former [section on] Buddha-nature pertains to the past;

it concerns principle, correctness, and causes, referring to a single Buddha's name, which is shallow and limited. These [good roots] belong to beginners. This [present section], however, encompasses both the present and practice.

The "Liao" (Understanding), "Yuan" (Conditions), and the six Buddhas Sūtra contain profound and vast merit and virtue. As for the "final mind," the Sūtra explains the reliance on the primary and secondary [realms], vows, and practices;

these are called the names of the Buddhas of the six directions. Hearing them constitutes the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); receiving them constitutes the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); and upholding them constitutes the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

The above [sections] have concluded. Next, the benefits of the Dharma obtained are revealed. Regarding "protection" (*anurakṣaṇā*) and "mindfulness" (*smṛti*): according to the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, there are six conditions.

First is the condition of differentiation, which is protection. Second is the condition of equality, which is mindfulness. The former condition further has two aspects: first, the proximate condition, which is mindfulness.

Because it is liberated with speed, it is the second, the distant condition, which is *samvara* (protection). Because it is delivered after a long period, there are two further types of near and distant conditions:
first, the condition for the increase of practice, which is *samvara*; second, the condition for receiving the Path, which is *smṛti* (mindfulness).
*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is here translated as "Unsurpassed Perfectly Equal and Right Enlightenment"; it is the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood. *Bodhi*...

"Ti" (提) translates as "the vehicle of humans and devas," which refers to the failure to awaken from the three miserable realms. "San" (三) translates as "the noble ones of the two vehicles—śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas"—which refers to the incorrectness of ordinary beings within the three realms.

Together with the preceding [character], this signifies entering emptiness from existence, contemplating the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and destroying the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*).

"Sarvajña" (一切智) means "all-knowing. "Miao" (藐) is translated as "inferior," referring to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) which is unequal in its self-benefit; it refers to the initial stage of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) which teaches people through provisional teachings.
"San" (三) is translated as "provisional," referring to the Three Vehicles that deliver others, yet are not yet ultimate; it refers to the final, real teaching of the Great Vehicle.

Combining these two, one emerges from emptiness into the provisional, contemplating the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and shattering the sands of ignorance; this is the "knowledge of the paths" (mārgajñatā). "Anuttara" (耨多羅) is translated as "gradual teaching" regarding the nature [of reality].
This has not yet reached the highest. It refers to those of the Sudden Teaching of the One Vehicle. "A" (阿) translates as "partial";

it refers to Buddhas of the Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle whose mind-nature within the Dharma-realm has not yet reached the ultimate unsurpassed state. Furthermore, it involves the perfect fusion of emptiness and existence, contemplating the Middle Way and the First Noble Truth, thereby shattering ignorance;
this is the All-Knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). Regarding the "Non-retrogressive," the *Dharmakara-praṇidhāna* states: "Upon hearing..."

I have finished naming them. Were there anyone who could regress from Bodhi, I would not attain perfect enlightenment; how much more so for those who hear the names of the Buddhas and uphold this sutra?
Compared to the aforementioned *avivartika* (non-regressing) state, the former refers to those already born [in the future], while the latter refers to those currently living but yet to be born.
Furthermore, this clearly elucidates the names of the sutras, each possessing the three types of wisdom and the six causes of benefit, each of which has its own manifestation.

By "my words," I refer to the *Sūtra of One Amitābha* spoken by the Buddha. By "all Buddhas," I refer to the six Buddhas who praised, exhorted, protected, and remembered [Amitābha] so that the fruit may be attained.
Through the analogy of faith, hearing, and aspiration, the increase [of merit] can be known. The benefits obtained are profound and deep. [This is stated] twice.

*Bodhi*. "Vow" (*praṇidhāna*) refers to wishing, aspiring, and seeking; "desire" (*chanda*) refers to delighting in and yearning for [the goal].

"Past, present, and future" refers to the three time periods. This signifies the three types of generating the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*), reveals the three causes, and accomplishes the three states of Buddhahood. Furthermore:
One should practice faith, conduct, and vows, generating them from time to time; they must not be abandoned for even a moment.

The phrase "these various lower [stages]" refers to attaining the fruit and not retreating from Bodhi; this distinguishes them from the aforementioned [stages]. The former refers to the path of instruction, specifically the first seven stages (*bhūmi*);

Regarding those buddha-fields—whether one has already been born there, is being born now, or will be born in the future—may all subsequent practices be fulfilled so that there is not a single person who is not born [there].

Those who now make the vow to be born include the Bodhisattvas from this world and fourteen other Buddha-fields under the guidance of Bhaiṣajyaguru Buddha, as well as Śāriputra, the Bhikṣu Ānanda, and Lady Vaidehī. Those who shall make the vow to be born include Maitreya Buddha.
After the passing of the Bodhisattvas Nāgārjuna and Aśvaghoṣa and the Bhikṣu Kambala of Northern India, humans and devas have examined various sūtras and śāstras in detail and synthesized them above.

My own discourse and the various other teachings each provide three types of provisions, six causes of benefit, and respective stages of non-retrogression, the attainment of enlightenment, the vision of the Buddha, and rebirth—these being the eight fruits of benefit. Reflect upon this carefully. Next, the concluding exhortation:
Therefore, Śāriputra, all sons and daughters of good family who possess faith should make a vow to be born in that land.

The two characters "therefore" conclude the preceding discussion on how the fruit of making a vow after believing in the Buddha is attained, and how birth in that place brings further benefit. All sons of good family...
The following section exhorts [the practitioner] to cultivate faith, aspiration, and practice; it differs slightly from the preceding portion.

In the preceding section, one has faith in the Buddha’s teaching, aspires to be born in that direction, and practices mindfulness of the Buddha with the understanding that one will attain enlightenment in the present life.

Here, however, one has faith in Amitābha, aspiring to see the Buddha, and aspires to be born in that direction with the understanding that one shall attain Buddhahood by practicing the recitation of the Name. Furthermore, the preceding section cites scriptural testimony.
"Exhortation by means of instruction": this refers to exhortation through the direct realization of the entire reality. Furthermore, it summarizes and concludes the preceding points to clarify them:
first, hearing of the merits of the environment and its inhabitants to exhort the aspiration; second, hearing that the Buddha manifests upon holding the name to exhort the aspiration;

third, hearing that the Buddhas protect one from falling back by merely hearing the name of the sutra to exhort faith; and fourth, hearing that by believing the teaching one achieves awakening and birth [in the Pure Land] to exhort the aspiration.

"Quàn-quàn" (exhortation) is pronounced with the *bèi* rhyme; "yuàn-yuàn" (vow) becomes ever deeper. Thus we know that faith, vow, and practice constitute the true cause, while birth in the Buddha-land is the actual fruit.
As for the stage, it is no longer merely the three non-regressions; one has already reached the position of being "one birth away from Buddhahood.
Compared to the previous men and women—though their ten excellences were superior—when added to these current twelve causes and sixteen fruits, how could the subsequent not surpass the preceding?

To call these "all good" (sarva-kuśala)—what praise could there be greater than this? △ Fourth, the section clarifying the three difficulties that lead to the realization of the fruit. Regarding the three difficulties of all Buddhas:

first, the manifestation of the broad and long tongue; second, the speaking of truthful words; third, the exhortation for sentient beings to have faith. Internally, there are again three difficulties:
first, the praise of Śākyamuni Buddha; second, the merits of Amitābha; third, the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas. Explanation.

Regarding the threefold difficulty of the Honored One: first, the performance of difficult practices; second, the attainment of the fruit that is difficult to obtain; and third, the teaching of the Dharma that is difficult to believe.

Internally, there are likewise three difficulties: first, the supreme virtues of Amitābha; second, the praise and protection of the six Buddhas; and third, the attainment of Buddhahood through the recitation of the name.
Within this, there are three parts. First, the Buddhas have already been praised.
Śāriputra, just as I now extol the inconceivable merits of the Buddhas, so too did they praise one another.
There are three praises. First, citing evidence from the six directions to encourage faith; this is the first praise, which reveals that those who hear of the Buddhas do not regress.
Second, the second praise, which exhorts the assembly to believe the teachings of the six Buddhas. Third, the third praise, concerning the inconceivable virtues of the six Buddhas.

Generally speaking, these collectively extol the Dharma-gate of the Buddha-remembrance method of the Western Pure Land; specifically, they open up ten aspects, namely, the simultaneous voices throughout the lands.
They issue from the same tongue; they share the same broad and long [tongue]; they share the same universal coverage; they share the same words of truth; they address the same assembly;
they share the same exhortation to believe; they share the same collective praise; they share the same name and virtue; and they share the same protective mindfulness.
△ Second, the various Buddhas having finished their praise, in two parts: first, the formal presentation.
Those Buddhas likewise praised my inconceivable merit. "The Buddhas" refers to the Buddhas of the six directions;
"and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the Buddhas of the four intermediate points and the three periods of time. There are also three types of praise:

first, the proclamation by the Buddhas of the Śākya lineage when they preach this sutra; second, the exhortation for the assembly to believe and hear this sutra; and third, their protective mindfulness of it.

The person who upholds this sutra is praised three times. "The virtues of my Buddha are inconceivable" is a general praise for the adornment and purity of the Land of Bliss and the benefits of the Buddha-dharma of reciting the name.
Specifically, there are ten aspects: performing difficult deeds; dwelling in the Sahā world; emerging from the five turbidities; attaining Bodhi;
acting for the sake of sentient beings; preaching the Dharma of this sutra; teaching the mindfulness of the Buddha; demonstrating the recitation of the name; and praising the six [perfections].
[The Buddha] first exhorted [the assembly] to believe and hear [his words]. Next, he explained in detail, saying:
"Śākyamuni Buddha is able to perform a most difficult and rare feat;

he is able, within the Sahā world-system, amidst the five turbidities of this evil age—the turbidity of the kalpa, the turbidity of views, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, and the turbidity of life—[to manifest his great power]."
Having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, [the Buddha] preaches for the sake of all sentient beings this Dharma that is difficult for the entire world to believe.

The first phrase is capable of praising; it constitutes the praise spoken by the six Buddhas. Regarding the second part, which explains what is praised below, first we cite that which is difficult to obtain.
Regarding this person: Śākyamuni—“Śākya” here translated as “Able Benevolent One”—refers to his clan name, for he possesses great compassion that benefits all beings.

“Muni”—here translated as “Silent Sage”—refers to his personal name, for his great wisdom is in profound accord with the principle of reality. Next, the extraordinary deeds are praised: “Able” refers to the capacity to undertake;

“to act” refers to the accomplishment of tasks; “rare” refers to self-awakening; “extremely difficult” refers to awakening others; and “meritorious deeds” refers to his activities. These are the foremost.
The practices are difficult to perform. *Sahā* means "Endurance" in this [language]. The sufferings of this land are the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
The evils of the world consist of the defilements of five matters, which are called the five turbidities. That which is summoned and brought forth by evil karma is called an "evil world.
This distinguishes it from the blissful land of *An-yang* (Sukhāvatī), which is an age of the five purities and virtues. In Sanskrit, *kalpa* means "time period. When it decreases to...

For twenty thousand years, the four turbidities converge; this is called the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). It results from the failure to distinguish between emptiness and the view [of self] within the mind of awakened clarity.

When form is freed from the four entanglements, the turbidity of the eon is cleared. Because of the five sharp afflictions (*kleśa*), various views blaze forth; this is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).
It results from the great delusion that forms the faculties within the mind. When one perceives emptiness as being devoid of self and dharmas, the turbidity of views is cleared.

Conditioned by the five dull afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), the obstruction of dust-like sands is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). This is caused by the mutual entanglement of the nature and characteristics within the mind.

When one perceives liberation from worldly toil, the turbidity of afflictions clears. Seeing the retribution of the aggregates of pride and ignorance, along with evil reputations and foul appellations, is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).
This is caused by the mind’s shifting and lingering, unable to abide. When conduct is free from arising and ceasing, the turbidity of sentient beings clears. As for form (*rūpa*)...

The mind’s continuity hastens the years and shortens the lifespan; this is called the turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*). It arises because the mind loses its standard for distinguishing between the same and the different.
When consciousness transcends the six [senses], the turbidity of life is cleared. To attain *trī-bodhi* within an age of the five turbidities—is this not difficult?

In contrast to the former two [turbidities], which belong to the stage of causal cultivation and partial realization, this belongs to the stage of fruition and ultimate completion. To be self-awakened to this is— [Note: The final phrase "is—" indicates the sentence is incomplete in the source text.]
The second is the difficulty of attaining the Way. Sentient beings—those of the three vehicles and the seven realms of existence—are like infants and fools.

The afflictions and obstacles of the turbid world are like throwing ashes and soil into water, which then becomes murky. All things—the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), the world of the vessel (*bhājana-loka*), and the world of awakening (*vijñāna-loka*)—are difficult to believe.

It is the Buddha-remembrance dharma. It is like the water-clearing pearl. The Buddha is like the village elder or headman who can, among sentient beings, preach the dharma that is difficult to believe;
his merit in awakening others is inconceivable. This is the third difficulty: the difficulty of preaching the Dharma.
The first [of the three] is general, while the latter two are specific; these are also brief explanations. If expanded, they become six: first, rare and marvelous deeds.

2. Enduring suffering in accordance with the masses; 3. Vowing to enter the turbid and evil world; 4. Establishing oneself to achieve fruition; 5. Universally bringing about transformation and deliverance;
6. Preaching the Dharma that is difficult to believe. △ Third, a summary of these difficult deeds.
Śāriputra, you should know that in this world of five turbidities, I have performed this difficult task:
having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I have preached this dharma so difficult to believe for the sake of all the worlds. This is truly most difficult.

This follows the words of praise from the various Buddhas to establish the reality [of the teaching]. However, there is a slight distinction. The praises of the aforementioned Buddhas concern solely the meritorious deeds of the resultant stage (*phala-avasthā*).
This account by Śākyamuni, however, encompasses both the vows and practices of the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*). First, regarding the "difficult-to-perform single practice":

in the causal stage, this refers to cultivating the practice of deliverance within the profound mind; in the resultant stage, it belongs to self-awakening (*sva-bodhi*). Second, regarding the "attainment of the difficult-to-attain fruit": in the causal stage...

Thus, when one’s upright mind accords with the Buddha-principle, the fruit belongs to perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). To preach the Dharma that is difficult to believe constitutes the cause;

After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, Śāriputra, the various bhikṣus, and all the devas, humans, asuras, and others in the world...
Ānanda and the others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and accepted it with faith;

they paid their respects and departed. The first phrase concludes the sūtra. "The assembly" below refers to those who heard [the teaching]. "Śāriputra" indicates the primary interlocutor. "The bhikṣus" refers to the rest of the community.
It encompasses those who constantly follow; the three vehicles and the fourfold assembly are all included therein. Humans, devas, and asuras constitute the three wholesome realms of existence.

Equally contained are the eight classes of beings and the seven difficulties. "Upon hearing" and below clarifies the practice and observance: hearing refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); rejoicing refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); receiving refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Thus, the Buddha is the pure speaker, and what he expounds is the pure Dharma that is turned. Following the rejoicing, the assembly attains [realization].
The fruit is purity. Faith is the provision of faith; receiving [the teaching] is the provision of aspiration; practice is the provision of application.

When these three provisions are complete, one’s rebirth in the Pure Land is certain. To "speak" is the teaching; to "rejoice" is the principle; to "believe" is the practice; to "pay homage" is the ritual.
This is the fruit. When the four dharma-gates are complete, one must surely awaken the people through this path.

"Root" (gēnběn) refers to the primary source to encompass its branches and secondary effects. It is an inconceivable spirit...

*Amṛta* means "immeasurable" (*amita*). *Bhāvi*, or alternatively *prabhāvi*, means "light. Combined, it means "Immeasurable Light," the Buddha of the Wisdom Body (*jñānakāya*). *Amṛtā*.
"Same as above, immeasurable" (*ananta*). "All attached to" (*sarva-rata*) or "all attained" (*sarva-siddha*);

This refers to the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha. *Amitābha-vikaraṇa* is to be understood as before. *Tā* means that True Suchness (*tathatā*) does not recede or move.

Taken together, this signifies "Immeasurable, Vast, and Great Life," wherein True Suchness and Dharma-nature are unmoving and unchanging; this is the Tathāgata-body Buddha. *Gama*.
*Ni* (Niti) is Sumeru; this is translated as "Ultimate Bliss" (*Sukhāvatī*), "Peaceful Nourishment," "Pure Tranquility," or "Sublime Intention.
*Gagana*, or alternatively *Ākāśa*, is translated as "Space"; it refers to the Heaven of Space in the western direction. Taken together, they mean the "Heavenly Realm of Ultimate Bliss.

Of these, the former four are the names of the Buddha, which constitute his primary retribution (*sambhogakāya*). This one is the name of the land, which constitutes his secondary retribution (*bhājanaloka*). *Kiṭa*—to speak fully:

This is explained in terms of the three provisions of faith, aspiration, and practice. *Svāhā* signifies swift and perfect accomplishment.
